title: When, Where and How
text:
Most people know the gap between intending to do something and actually doing it. The German psychologist Peter Gollwitzer proposed a simple bridge: an implementation intention, a plan in the form "When situation X arises, I will do Y." In 1997 he and Veronika Brandstatter published studies testing it.

In one study, university students in Germany were asked, just before the Christmas holidays, to write a report about how they spent Christmas Eve and to send it in within two days of the holiday. Some students were also asked to write down exactly when and where during those two days they would write the report. The others received no such instruction.

The difference was large. Students who had formed a specific plan were far more likely to deliver the report on time, more than twice as often as those who had not. The plan took only a minute to make, yet it made the moment of action easier to recognize and to seize when it came.

Other studies in the paper showed that people with implementation intentions acted more promptly when the planned opportunity arrived. Over the following decades, hundreds of studies tested the technique for goals ranging from exercise and healthy eating to cancer screenings and voting. A 2006 meta-analysis by Gollwitzer and Paschal Sheeran found a medium to large effect on goal attainment.
lesson: Turn a vague goal into a specific if-then plan: when, where and how you will act. Deciding the moment in advance makes it much more likely that you will act when it arrives.
source: Gollwitzer, P. M., and Brandstatter, V. (1997). Implementation intentions and effective goal pursuit. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 73(1), 186-199.
place: Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich, Germany
